summary: This unit teaches you to prepare the drawings a fabrication job is built from. You will learn to plan a drawing set, use standard lines, scales, lettering and title blocks, construct shapes accurately, and draw orthographic, auxiliary, sectional and pictorial views. You will also learn to add dimensions, tolerances and weld symbols, link an assembly drawing to its parts list and detail drawings, work in CAD, and check, approve, issue and revise drawings so that the workshop only ever builds from the current one.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). At Level 2 you learned to read drawings and make simple sketches. At Level 3 you **prepare finished drawings** that other people build from, you check drawings made by others, and you lead the drawing work on a job.

A workshop drawing is an instruction. If it is wrong, unclear or out of date, the steel is cut wrong, the welds are put on the wrong side, or a part will not fit on site, and the cost of the error grows at every stage. A good drawing lets the fitter make the job **without asking a single question**, and lets the inspector check it against clear sizes and limits.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust and other training centres who plan and lead fabrication work, and anyone who must draw gates, frames, brackets, supports and small structures for a workshop to make.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Plan the drawings for a job
Collect the site sizes, the client's needs and the material; decide which drawings are needed; choose sheet sizes, scales and views; sketch the layout first.
Use the right line types and widths, clear lettering, a full title block and the projection symbol, so every reader takes the same meaning.
Draw tangent arcs, rounded corners, slots, hexagons, bisectors and equal divisions with instruments or in CAD.
Draw the views a part needs
Orthographic views lined up correctly; auxiliary views of sloping faces; sectional views of hidden insides; pictorial views for clients and assemblers.
Give each size once, from sensible datums, with tolerances and fits that suit the job and no tighter.
Weld symbols with sizes, weld preparations, site welds, and a parts list linked to the assembly by item numbers.
Set up units, layers and the title block; draw full size; print to a stated scale; save under a controlled file name.
Check drawings against the brief, record errors, raise revisions, keep a drawing register and withdraw old copies.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on planning, standards, construction, projection, sections, dimensioning, tolerances, weld symbols, assembly drawings, pictorial views, CAD and checking.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms) and longer answers that explain how you would plan, draw, check or issue drawings.

**Practical tasks**: as a group, a hand-drawn set of workshop drawings for a welded bracket (assembly, parts list, details, a section, weld symbols, checking and a revision), and CAD drawings of a fabricated support with a section and an auxiliary view, printed to scale and checked.

blocks.note: Short-answer questions ask for exact words such as auxiliary view, half section, removed section, tangent point, bisector, datum, root face, balloon, exploded view, layer, layout and interference fit. Learn the key terms in the Revision section.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Most drawing errors start before the first line is drawn: a size not measured, a client need not asked about, a material not agreed. Plan first, then draw.

head: Information
Why you need it
Where it comes from
rows: It decides the sizes, sections and welds. Anything that carries people, vehicles or heavy loads (stairs, platforms, canopies, beams) is designed or approved by an engineer; you draw what the engineer specifies.
The client, the engineer, the design brief
So the item fits: openings, levels, existing steel, walls, where it fixes and what it fixes to.
A site visit with a tape; photos with the tape in view; existing drawings
Style, height, finish, colour, quantity, delivery date and budget.
Section sizes, grades, galvanising or paint system.
The engineer's specification, stock available locally
The drawing standard, the welding code or procedure, and any building rules the job must meet.
The Centre's procedures, the client's specification
Largest plate the shop can cut, bending and rolling capacity, lifting, and how the item will be transported.

blocks.note: Measure on site yourself whenever you can: walls and openings in older buildings are seldom square or level, so measure both diagonals and check levels. Jamaica uses metric units, but builders and clients often still talk in feet and inches. Convert carefully (1 inch = 25.4 mm; 1 foot = 304.8 mm) and draw in millimetres.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Drawing
What it shows
Typical scale
rows: The whole item put together: overall sizes, how the parts fit, welds made at assembly, a balloon for each part, and the parts list
Each part that must be made: every size, hole, bend, cut-out and weld preparation
Item number, description, size, material, length and quantity of every part
A table on the GA or on its own sheet
The lengths and pieces to cut from stock lengths and plates
Where the item goes on site and where it fixes
What the item will look like, for a client who cannot read orthographic views
Not to scale, or to a stated scale

head: Sheet
Size (mm)
Common use
rows: Most workshop details and small assemblies; easy to handle at the bench
Structural general arrangements and site drawings

blocks.p: Each size is half of the one above it: two A4 sheets side by side make an A3. Use the Centre's printed sheets or CAD template, with a border and a title block in the bottom right-hand corner.
A scale is written **drawing size : real size**. At 1:5, 1 mm on the paper stands for 5 mm on the job. At 2:1, the drawing is twice the real size.

head: Kind
Standard scales
Typical use
rows: Small features: grooves, weld preparations, small holes

ul: **Real size = size on the drawing × the scale factor.** At 1:20, a line 37.5 mm long stands for 37.5 × 20 = 750 mm. At 5:1, a groove drawn 12 mm wide is really 12 ÷ 5 = 2.4 mm.
Use the standard scales only. Odd scales such as 1:3 or 1:8 are hard to read with a scale rule and easy to misread.
Choose the **largest standard scale that lets all the views fit** on the sheet with room for dimensions, notes and the parts list.
Write the main scale in the title block. A view at a different scale has its own scale written under it, for example DETAIL B SCALE 5:1.
Never measure a print to find a size. Prints shrink or stretch, and some views are not to scale. Put DO NOT SCALE in the title block, and give every size the workshop needs as a written dimension.

blocks.h: Will it fit? A worked example

blocks.p: A frame is 1500 mm long, 600 mm deep and 800 mm high. You want a front view, a plan and an end view on an A3 sheet. Inside the border, with the title block taken out, you have about 390 mm across and 250 mm down for the views. Allow about 60 mm across and 60 mm down for the gaps between views and for dimensions.

head: Scale
Across the sheet (front + end + gaps)
Down the sheet (front + plan + gaps)
Fits?
rows: Yes, but small and hard to read

blocks.p: So 1:10 is the best choice: the largest standard scale that fits.
Every sheet carries a title block. A full one gives:

ul: The title of the drawing and the job or client name
The drawing number and sheet number (for example Sheet 2 of 5)
The revision letter or number
The scale, and the projection symbol
The units (ALL DIMENSIONS IN MILLIMETRES)
The material and finish, where one applies to the whole drawing
The general tolerances (for example UNLESS STATED ±1 mm)
Drawn by, checked by and approved by, each with a date
The Centre's or company's name
DO NOT SCALE

blocks.h: Plan the layout before you draw

flow: List the views each sheet needs
Work out the size of each view at the chosen scale
Sketch boxes for the views on scrap paper, with room for dimensions, notes, the parts list and the title block
If it does not fit, change the scale or the sheet size, or split the work over more sheets
Start the real drawing with light construction lines

blocks.note: At Level 3 you may lead other drafters. Before anyone starts, agree the standard, the template, the numbering, who draws and who checks each sheet, and the dates. Start the drawing register on day one.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A drawing standard is an agreed set of rules for lines, lettering, views, symbols and dimensions. When every drawing follows it, **every reader takes the same meaning** from it, whoever drew it. Use the standard the Centre chooses, and use it the same way on every sheet. Drawings from the USA follow American practice, and those from Britain and Europe follow ISO and British practice, so look at a drawing's notes and symbols before you read it.

head: Line
Looks like
Used for
rows: Short centre lines on small circles
Centre lines and lines of symmetry
Chain thin, thick at the ends and at changes of direction
As above, with short thick parts and arrows
Other positions of moving parts, such as a gate swung open
A wavy or zigzag thin line
Where a view is broken off, or the edge of a broken-out section

ul: Thick lines are about **twice as wide** as thin lines, so outlines stand out. Common pairs are 0.7 mm with 0.35 mm, and 0.5 mm with 0.25 mm.
With pencils, use a hard pencil (2H) for construction lines and thin lines, and a softer one (H or HB) for thick lines and lettering. With pens, use 0.35 mm and 0.7 mm.
Construction lines are drawn very lightly, so they disappear when the drawing is copied, or are rubbed out.
All finished lines must be dense and black so they still show on a photocopy or a scan.
Centre lines run about 3 mm past the outline. Long dashes cross at the centre of a circle. Dashes of hidden lines meet at corners.
Use **capital letters**, plain and upright (or with the slight slope the standard allows), all of one height for each use.
Typical heights: about 3.5 mm for notes and dimensions, and 5 or 7 mm for titles and drawing numbers.
Draw faint guide lines for hand lettering. Do not join letters, and leave clear spaces between words.
Why it matters: workshop prints get oily, dusty and copied many times. Clear capitals of one height stay readable when small, joined handwriting does not, and a misread figure means a wrong part.
In CAD, use the template's text style: a simple, plain font at standard heights.

head: Instrument
Used for
Care
rows: Drawing board with T-square or parallel motion
Horizontal lines; a square base for the set squares
Keep the working edge clean and undamaged; tape the sheet square at the corners
Vertical and angled lines; together with the T-square they give every 15° step
Never use them as a cutting edge
Keep the point and lead sharp; cap the point
Never use it as a straight edge for ruling or cutting
Small circles, isometric ellipses, even lettering
Keep them flat so they do not warp
Lines; clean corrections without smudging nearby lines
Keep pencils sharp; keep hands and instruments clean

blocks.note: Cap compass and divider points and keep craft knives closed when not in use. Sit upright, with the board at a comfortable height and good light, and take short breaks from close work. Keep sample parts and steel off the drawing boards.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Fabrication drawings are full of shapes made from straight lines and arcs: rounded corners on base plates, gussets, lifting lugs, slotted holes, hexagon bar and nuts. Constructing them correctly makes the outline smooth and the sizes right. The same geometry is what a CNC plasma or laser cutter follows when it cuts from a CAD file.

head: Construction
How to do it with instruments
rows: Bisect a line (find its middle, square to it)
Set the compass to more than half the line. Draw arcs above and below from each end. Join the two crossing points: that line is the **perpendicular bisector**.

From the corner, draw an arc cutting both arms. From those two points draw equal arcs that cross. A line from the corner through the crossing is the **bisector**: it splits the angle into two equal parts.
Draw a line parallel to another at a set distance
Slide a set square along the T-square, or draw two arcs of that radius from points on the line and draw a line touching both.
Divide a line into equal parts

From one end draw a line at any angle. Step off the number of equal parts along it with dividers. Join the last mark to the other end of the line, then draw lines parallel to it through the other marks.
Draw a circle whose diameter is the across-corners size. The side of a hexagon equals the radius, so step the radius round the circle six times and join the points.
Draw a circle whose diameter is the across-flats size, then draw six sides touching it with the 30°/60° set square. Across corners ≈ 1.155 × across flats.

blocks.h: Tangents: arcs that blend into lines and other arcs

blocks.p: An arc is **tangent** to a line when it touches the line and blends into it without crossing it. The point where they meet is the **tangent point**. If the line and the arc do not meet exactly there, the cut outline has a step or a kink.

head: Problem
How to find the arc's centre
Where the tangent points are
rows: Arc of radius R tangent to two straight lines (a rounded corner)
Draw a line parallel to each straight line, R inside it. They cross at the centre.
Draw a line from the centre square to each straight line; the foot of each is a tangent point.
Arc of radius R touching a line and the outside of a circle of radius r
Draw a line parallel to the straight line, R away. Draw an arc of radius r + R from the circle's centre. They cross at the centre.
On the line square from the centre to the straight line, and on the line joining the two centres.
Arc of radius R enclosing a circle of radius r (touching it inside)
As above, but use radius R − r from the circle's centre.
On the line joining the two centres, extended.
A slot (two semicircles joined by straight sides)
Mark the two arc centres the slot length apart; draw the end arcs at half the slot width.
Draw the straight sides touching both arcs; the tangent points lie straight across from each centre.

flow: Draw all centre lines and the arc centres lightly
Find every tangent point and mark it with a short thin line
Line in the arcs first
Line in the straight lines into the arcs, stopping exactly at the tangent points
Check the outline is smooth, with no steps, gaps or overlaps

blocks.note: It is easier to join a straight line neatly to an arc than an arc to a line, so draftsmen line in arcs first. In CAD, the fillet command and the tangent and perpendicular object snaps find the tangent points exactly. Never judge a join by eye and leave a tiny gap: a CNC cutter needs a closed outline.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A lug plate has a Ø30 hole with an R40 rounded end, and straight sides that run down to a 160 mm wide base. Draw the hole's centre lines and the Ø30 circle; draw the R40 arc from the same centre; draw the base line and mark its ends; draw each side from the end of the base so that it just touches the R40 arc. The tangent point is where a line from the hole's centre, square to the side, meets the arc. Line in the arc first, then the sides, stopping at the tangent points.

In orthographic projection each view looks **square onto** one side of the object. The usual views are the **front view** (front elevation), the **plan** (looking down from above) and the **end view** (side elevation). Each view shows two of the three main sizes:

head: View
Shows
Lines up with
rows: The plan (the same length) and the end view (the same height)

blocks.p: So the front view and the plan are lined up one above the other, and the front view and the end view are lined up side by side. The depth, which the plan and the end view share, is carried across with a 45° line or with compasses or dividers.

head: Point
First angle projection
Third angle projection
rows: The view from the left is drawn
On the right of the front view
On the left of the front view
The view from the right is drawn
On the left of the front view
On the right of the front view
Each view goes on the far side of the front view from where you looked
Each view goes on the same side as where you looked

blocks.p: Both methods are used in Jamaica, so every drawing must carry the **projection symbol**: a cone with its tip cut off, drawn in two views. The symbols for the two methods differ in where the end view of the cone sits. Learn the symbol on the Centre's sheets, and always add it near the title block. A fitter who assumes the wrong method will put a hole, a cleat or a weld on the wrong side.

ul: Choose as the front view the view that shows **most of the shape**, with the fewest hidden lines, usually with the longest side across the sheet and the item the way it stands in use.
Draw only the views needed to show the shape fully. A flat plate may need one view and a note such as 10 THK PLATE. A round bar may need one view, with Ø before its size.
Show hidden edges with thin dashed lines where they help. When hidden lines crowd a view, use a section instead.

blocks.p: A face that slopes to the normal views looks **foreshortened** in them: shorter than it really is. Holes in it look like ellipses, and none of its sizes can be read off. To show its **true shape and size**, draw an **auxiliary view**, projected looking square onto the sloping face.

flow: Draw the view in which the sloping face shows as a straight edge (its edge view)
Draw projection lines from the corners and hole centres, square (at 90°) to that edge
Draw a reference line parallel to the edge, a convenient distance away
Measure each depth from the matching reference line in the plan or end view and transfer it with dividers
Join the points; holes now show as true circles and can be dimensioned
Usually draw only the sloping face (a partial auxiliary view) and break it off with a freehand line

blocks.note: A sloping edge shows its true length only in a view where it lies parallel to the paper. That is why an auxiliary view is projected from the view in which the face is seen edge-on.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Kind
How it is drawn
Good for
rows: Three axes: one upright and two at 30° to the horizontal. Lengths along the three axes are drawn true (isometric drawing). Circles become ellipses.
Showing clients and assemblers what the item looks like
The front face drawn true shape; depth lines at 45°, often at half length (cabinet oblique) so the item does not look too deep
Parts with circles or curves on one face
The parts drawn pulled apart along the lines where they fit together, still in line
Assembly instructions; showing how parts go together

ul: Isometric circles are drawn as ellipses. The **four-centre method** draws a good approximate ellipse quickly with a compass, using four arcs; an ellipse template or plotted points also work.
Only lines parallel to the three isometric axes are drawn true length; a sloping line is found by plotting its two ends.
When you dimension an isometric view, draw each dimension line **parallel to the edge it measures**, with projection lines parallel to the isometric axes.
Pictorial views usually carry only the main sizes. The workshop builds from the orthographic drawings.

blocks.note: Many clients cannot read orthographic views: a householder in Portmore ordering a grille, or a church board choosing a gate. Show them a pictorial or 3D view with the main sizes and the finish, talk them through it, and have them sign and date the approved copy before workshop drawings are issued. Check that the workshop drawings match what was approved.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: When the inside of an item is hidden by its outside, hidden lines pile up and confuse. A **sectional view** shows the item as if it were cut along a **cutting plane** and the near part taken away, so inside edges show as clear solid lines and the cut faces are hatched.

ul: The **cutting plane** is a thin chain line, thick at its ends and wherever it changes direction, with arrows showing the direction of viewing and a letter at each end (A–A).
The view is titled under it: SECTION A–A.
Cut faces are **hatched** with thin lines, usually at 45°, evenly spaced: about 3–4 mm apart on an average part, closer on small parts.
Two parts touching each other are hatched in **opposite directions** (or at a different spacing), so the joint between them shows.
One part is hatched the same way in every view of that drawing.
Very thin cut parts, such as sheet, gaskets or thin plate at a small scale, are filled in **solid black**, with a small white gap between neighbouring parts.
Visible edges beyond the cutting plane are drawn; hidden lines are usually left out.

blocks.h: Parts not hatched when the plane runs along them

blocks.p: These are drawn in outline, not hatched, when the cutting plane runs **along their length**: bolts, nuts, screws, washers, rivets, pins, keys and solid shafts, and also ribs, webs and gussets. Hatching them would make them look like solid lumps: a bracket with a hatched gusset looks like a solid block, which gives the wrong idea of its shape. When the plane cuts straight **across** them, they are hatched as normal.

head: Section
What it is
Typical use
rows: The plane cuts right through the whole item
A welded box, a flanged pipe spool, a hopper
A quarter is cut away: one half shows the outside, the other half the inside, divided by a centre line
Symmetrical parts such as flanges, round covers and pulleys: it saves a view
A stepped cutting plane passes through features that are not in one line; the steps are not shown in the section
Holes or slots in a plate that are not in a straight line
The cross-section is turned through 90° and drawn on the view itself, with a thin outline
The shape of an arm, rib or rolled section along its length
Like a revolved section, but drawn away from the view, labelled with its cutting plane letters, and often at a larger scale
When there is no room on the view, or the shape must be enlarged
A small part cut away, bounded by a freehand break line
One hole, recess or weld on an otherwise plain part

blocks.note: Choose the section that shows the inside with the least drawing. A half section shows inside and outside in one view; a revolved or removed section saves a whole extra view; a broken-out section shows one feature without cutting the whole part.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Give **every size** needed to make and check the part, and give each size **once only**. A size shown twice may be changed in one place and not the other.
Dimension each feature in the view that shows its true shape: a hole where it shows as a circle; a sloping face in its auxiliary view.
Do not dimension to hidden lines.
Put dimensions outside the view where you can, with smaller sizes nearer the view and larger ones outside them, so that lines do not cross.
Projection lines are thin, start with a small gap (about 1 mm) from the outline, and run about 2–3 mm past the dimension line.
Dimension lines are thin, with neat filled arrowheads (about 3 mm long) touching the projection lines. Never use an outline or a centre line as a dimension line.

Write sizes in millimetres without "mm", and state ALL DIMENSIONS IN MILLIMETRES in the title block. Place the figures above the line, so they read from the bottom or the right of the sheet, or all horizontal, as the standard says.
Leave nothing for the fitter to work out by adding or taking away sizes.
A size given only for information is put in brackets, for example (1200). It is not used for checking.

head: On the drawing
Meaning
rows: Six Ø18 holes, equally spaced on a pitch circle of 150 mm diameter (the circle through their centres)

blocks.p: A **datum** is an edge, face or centre line from which other sizes are measured. Choose datums the fitter can find and measure from easily: a straight sheared or machined edge, or the centre line of a symmetrical part.

head: Method
How
Effect
rows: Each size runs from the last feature to the next

Small errors **add up** along the chain. If each of three chained sizes may be 1 mm out, the third hole can be 3 mm from where it should be. Use chains only where the distance between neighbouring features is what matters.
Every size runs from the same datum
Errors do not build up: each feature is within its own tolerance. The fitter marks every feature from one edge. Best for hole patterns and base plates.

blocks.p: No part is made to an exact size. A **tolerance** says how far a size may vary; the **limits** are the largest and smallest sizes allowed.

head: How it is written
Example
Limits
rows: General tolerance in the title block
UNLESS STATED ±1 mm ON LENGTHS, ±1° ON ANGLES
Applies to every size that has no tolerance of its own

ul: Set each tolerance **as loose as the job allows**. Tight limits need slower methods, machining, more checking and more rejects, so they cost time and money. A welded gate frame might be ±2 mm; a hole for a turning pin needs a few tenths or hundredths of a millimetre.
Welding pulls parts out of line. Where holes must line up with another part, the drawing often says to drill or machine them **after welding**.

head: Fit
Hole and shaft
How it behaves
Example
rows: The hole is always bigger than the shaft
Gate pivot pin, hinge pin, sliding bolt
The limits overlap: a pair may be slightly loose or slightly tight
Locates accurately; tapped or lightly pressed in
The shaft is always bigger than the hole
Must be pressed, driven or shrunk in; stays fixed
A bush pressed into a lug

blocks.p: To decide the fit from the limits: if the **smallest hole** is not smaller than the **largest shaft**, it is a clearance fit. If the **largest hole** is smaller than the **smallest shaft**, it is an interference fit. Otherwise it is a transition fit.

Worked example: a bush is bored Ø40 +0.10/+0.02 (40.02 to 40.10) and its pin is Ø40 −0.03/−0.09 (39.91 to 39.97). Smallest clearance = 40.02 − 39.97 = 0.05 mm; largest = 40.10 − 39.91 = 0.19 mm. There is always clearance, so it is a clearance fit.

blocks.note: Machinists often write fits with ISO letters and numbers, such as H7/g6: a capital letter for the hole and a small letter for the shaft. Look the limits up in the table of fits the Centre uses.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: What a weld symbol tells the welder

blocks.p: The drawing must show **every weld**: where it is, which side, what type, what size, and anything special. Weld symbols do this in a small space, so nobody has to guess. The Centre uses AWS welding symbols (the AWS standard for welding symbols). British and European drawings may use the ISO system, which looks similar but is read differently, so check which one a drawing uses.

head: Part of the symbol
What it does
rows: Points to the joint. The side of the joint it touches is the **arrow side**.
The horizontal line the arrow joins. The weld symbols sit on it.
The type of weld: a triangle for a fillet, a V for a single-V groove, and so on.
Weld on both sides of the joint
For a fillet, the leg size (for example 6); for a groove weld, the depth of preparation or weld size
Length and pitch, right of the symbol
For an intermittent weld, for example 50-150: 50 mm welds at 150 mm centres
The angle (for example 60°) near the symbol; the root opening written inside it
Circle at the bend of the arrow
**Weld all round**, for example a post welded right round to a base plate
Flag at the bend of the arrow
**Field weld**: made on site, not in the shop
The finished shape of the weld face (flat, convex or concave) and how it is finished (for example G for grinding)
A reference such as the WPS number or the process; left off when not needed

head: Weld
Symbol shape
Note
rows: Right-angled triangle, upright side on the left
The most common weld in fabrication
Thin plate butt welds with square edges
One upright line and one sloping line
Only one plate is bevelled; the arrow points to that plate (with a break in the arrow if needed)
A U, or a J shape
Thick plate, less weld metal than a V
Weld through a hole or slot in the top plate
A small half circle on the opposite side
A run on the back of a groove weld

blocks.note: In the ISO system a dashed line runs alongside the reference line, and whether the symbol sits on the solid line or the dashed line decides the side. ISO fillet sizes have a letter: "a" for the throat and "z" for the leg, so a5 and z7 are about the same weld. Never read an ISO symbol with AWS rules.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: For a full-penetration butt weld the drawing shows the preparation: the **bevel angle** on each plate (for example 30°, giving a 60° included angle), the **root face** (the small flat left at the bottom of the bevel, for example 1.5 mm), the **root gap** (for example 2 mm), and any backing bar. Put them on the weld symbol or in an enlarged detail (for example DETAIL B SCALE 5:1).

ul: **Why:** the joint must be cut and set up as designed, or the welder cannot get full penetration and the joint will not be as strong as the design assumes.
The inspector checks fit-up and the finished weld against the same sizes, so the drawing is also the **acceptance standard**.
General notes save repeating symbols, for example ALL FILLET WELDS 6 mm UNLESS NOTED, WELD TO WPS-03, or the inspection the welds need.

The **general arrangement** shows the whole item assembled, with overall sizes, the welds made at assembly, and a **balloon** for each part: a small circle with the item number, on a leader that ends in a dot on the part.
Number the balloons in a clear order (for example in the order of assembly) and line them up neatly.

The **parts list** gives, for each item number: description, section size, material and grade, length, quantity, and the detail drawing number. Full section sizes such as 40 × 40 × 3 SHS or 6 THK PLATE go here, so the store can issue the steel and the estimator can price it.
A **detail drawing** gives every size needed to make one part, with its item number, material, quantity and finish.
Bought-in standard parts (bolts, hinges, castors, couplings) are listed with their specification but not detailed.

flow: Balloon on the GA (item 4)
Line 4 in the parts list: description, size, material, quantity, detail drawing number
Detail drawing of item 4: every size needed to make it
Cutting list: the pieces to cut
Part marked 4 in the workshop and fitted where the GA shows

blocks.note: Every sheet in the set carries the same job name and number system, so a part can be followed from the GA to its detail and back.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Setting
What to do
Why
rows: The workshop works in millimetres; sizes come out right
Draw every part **full size** (1:1) in model space
Measured and dimensioned sizes are true; files for CNC cutting are right; the scale is set only when printing
One layer for each kind of line or item: outlines, hidden, centre lines, dimensions, hatching, text, weld symbols, border
Each layer carries the right line type and width, so thick and thin lines print properly; any layer can be switched off or locked
Start from the Centre's template with the border, title block, text and dimension styles
Every drawing looks the same and nothing is left off
Set out the sheet, title block and viewports at a standard scale
The print matches the scale written in the title block
Endpoint, midpoint, centre, intersection, tangent, perpendicular
Drawing number and revision in the file name, for example J0425-03-B; saved in the agreed folder and backed up
The right version is always found and nothing is lost

blocks.p: CAD makes changes quick, copies repeated parts exactly, keeps geometry exact, and can export outlines for CNC plasma or laser cutting. It does not check itself: a CAD drawing still needs a checker.

blocks.note: A CNC cutter follows the lines exactly as drawn. Draw the part outline as a closed shape at exact size, on its own layer, with no gaps, overlaps or doubled lines, and keep dimensions and text off the cutting layer. The cutting machine's software normally allows for the width of the cut; agree this with the operator.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Print from the layout at **100%**. "Fit to page" shrinks or stretches the drawing, so the print no longer matches the scale in the title block.
Check every print: measure a known size with a scale rule and compare it with the scale in the title block. A scale bar on the sheet helps.

blocks.p: A drawing is checked by **a second person** before it is issued: a fresh eye finds errors the drafter has stopped seeing. An error found on paper costs minutes; the same error found in cut steel costs hours and material.

head: Check
What to look for
rows: Title, numbers, revision, scale, projection symbol, units, material, finish, tolerances, names and dates
Right views, correctly projected and lined up; correct line types
Cutting planes labelled; hatching correct; ribs, bolts and shafts not hatched along their length
Every size given once, from sensible datums; chains add up to the overall size; holes match the mating part
Present where needed and not tighter than necessary
A symbol for every weld, the right side, the size, preparations, field welds
Every balloon has a line; sizes, materials and quantities match the details

flow: Compare the drawing with the brief, sketch or sample
Work through the check sheet
Mark each error on a print in red
Talk the errors through with the drafter, so they learn
The drafter corrects the drawing
Check the corrections
Sign and date the checked box
The approver signs; the drawing is issued

ul: Until it is approved, a drawing is marked PRELIMINARY, FOR APPROVAL or NOT FOR CONSTRUCTION, so nobody makes parts from it.

When a drawing changes after issue, **raise the revision** (A to B, for example) in the title block, and add a line to the revision table: the revision, what changed, the date, who changed it and who checked it. Mark the changed area with a cloud or a small triangle with the revision letter.
The **drawing register** lists every drawing: its number, title, current revision and date, and who was given which revision.
When a new revision is issued, collect the old copies from everyone the register lists, and destroy them or stamp them SUPERSEDED. Keep one marked copy of each old revision on file as a record.

blocks.note: Workshop staff often photograph drawings with their phones and share them in group chats. A photo of an old revision is still an old revision. When you issue a change, tell everyone it replaces the old sheet and ask them to delete old photos.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: Agree the standard, template and numbering before anyone starts.
Share the sheets by skill, and give each sheet a checker who did not draw it.
Use a check sheet so every drawing is checked the same way.
When a junior repeats a mistake, explain why it matters, show how to put it right, and add the point to the check sheet.
Keep the register up to date, and keep to the dates set in the job plan.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can list the information to collect before drawing, and plan the drawings a job needs.
I can choose a sheet size and the largest standard scale that fits, and work out real sizes from a scale.
I can fill in a title block fully, including the projection symbol and general tolerances.
I can use the right line types and widths, and letter clearly.
I can bisect lines and angles, divide a line into equal parts, and construct hexagons.
I can find the centre and tangent points of an arc that blends into lines or circles.
I can draw front, plan and end views lined up in first or third angle projection.
I can project an auxiliary view to show the true shape of a sloping face.
I can choose and draw full, half, offset, revolved, removed and broken-out sections, with correct hatching.
I can dimension a part from datums, each size once, with the right symbols.
I can read and set tolerances, and tell clearance, transition and interference fits apart.
I can draw AWS weld symbols with sizes, sides, preparations, field welds and weld-all-round.
I can link an assembly drawing, its balloons, parts list and detail drawings.
I can draw isometric, oblique and exploded views and dimension an isometric view.
I can set up a CAD drawing with units, layers, template, layout and a controlled file name, and print it to scale.
I can check another person's drawing, record the errors, and sign it off.
I can raise a revision, keep a drawing register and withdraw old copies.

terms: Auxiliary view
A view projected square to a sloping face, to show its true shape
Balloon
A numbered circle on a leader that links a part on an assembly drawing to the parts list
Bisector
A line that divides an angle (or a line) into two equal parts
Chain dimensioning
Sizes given from one feature to the next, so errors can add up
Clearance fit
A fit in which the hole is always bigger than the shaft
Cutting plane
The line showing where an item is imagined cut for a section
Datum
The edge, face or line from which other sizes are measured
Detail drawing
A drawing giving every size needed to make one part
Drawing register
The list of every drawing with its current revision and who holds which copy
Exploded view
A pictorial view with the parts drawn apart along the lines where they fit
First angle projection
The method in which the plan goes below the front view and the view from the left goes on the right
Foreshortened
Looking shorter than true because the face or edge slopes away from the viewer
General arrangement (GA)
The drawing of the whole item assembled
Half section
A view showing half the part cut open and half as an outside view
Hatching
Thin, evenly spaced lines showing a cut surface in a section
Interference fit
A fit in which the shaft is always bigger than the hole, so it must be pressed in
Isometric
A pictorial view with axes upright and at 30° to the horizontal
Layer
A level in CAD that groups one kind of item, such as outlines or dimensions
Layout
The CAD space (paper space) where the sheet, title block and print scale are set out
Limits
The largest and smallest sizes a tolerance allows
Parts list
The table of every part: item number, description, size, material and quantity
PCD
Pitch circle diameter: the circle through the centres of a ring of holes
Removed section
A section drawn away from the main view, labelled with its cutting plane letters
Revision
A numbered or lettered change to an issued drawing, recorded in its revision table
Revolved section
A cross-section turned through 90° and drawn on the view itself
Root face
The small flat left at the bottom of a bevelled plate edge
Scale
The ratio of drawing size to real size
Tangent point
The point where an arc meets a line or another arc smoothly, touching without crossing
Third angle projection
The method in which the plan goes above the front view and the view from the right goes on the right
Title block
The panel giving the drawing's title, number, revision, scale, names and other key facts
Tolerance
The amount a size may vary from the size given
Weld symbol
The standard sign on a drawing giving a weld's type, side, size and other details

c1.title: A jerk-pan stand for a cook shop in Boston, Portland
c1.text: Nadine, a Level 3 trainee, is drawing a steel stand for a jerk pan at a cook shop in Boston, Portland. The stand is 1700 mm long overall, 650 mm deep and 900 mm high, including a side shelf that folds down when not in use. A drip tray under the pan slopes towards a drain hole. She wants a front view, a plan and an end view on one A3 sheet, where she has about 390 mm across and 250 mm down for the views, and she allows about 60 mm each way for the gaps between views and for dimensions.

c2.title: Checking base plates for bus-shelter posts in Falmouth
c2.text: The parish council has ordered six bus shelters for Falmouth, Trelawny. Jodi-Ann, a junior in the drawing office, has drawn the 300 × 300 × 12 mm base plate for the posts, and Mr Clarke asks you to check it. The four holes are dimensioned from the left edge to the first hole and then from hole to hole. The overall width is shown in both the plan and the end view. The holes are drawn Ø22 +0.5/0 for the holding-down bolts, and the title block gives a general tolerance of ±1 mm.

c3.title: A coffee-pulper hopper near Mavis Bank
c3.text: A farmers' group near Mavis Bank, St Andrew, has asked the Centre to make a hopper that feeds coffee cherries into a pulping machine. The hopper is made of 3 mm sheet with four sloping sides and a stiffening plate welded inside. Its bottom flange is bolted to the pulper through eight Ø14 holes equally spaced on a 400 mm pitch circle. The front side slopes at 60° and has a square inspection hatch in it. The general arrangement is drawn at 1:10.

c4.title: A water-tank tower for a basic school in Highgate
c4.text: Dwight is producing CAD drawings of a steel tower for two water tanks at a basic school in Highgate, St Mary. The four 100 × 100 × 4 mm SHS columns are welded right round to their base plates in the shop with 6 mm fillets. The cross-bracing is bolted up and then welded on site. Revision A was issued to the workshop last week; the school has since asked for the tower to be 300 mm taller, and Dwight has prepared Revision B.

c5.title: Lifting lugs for a boat davit in Old Harbour Bay
c5.text: The fishermen's co-operative in Old Harbour Bay, St Catherine, wants a small davit to lift outboard engines. Kemoy is drawing the details by hand: a lifting lug with a Ø30 hole, an R40 rounded end and straight sides running down to a 160 mm base, and a pivot made from 24 mm across-flats hexagon bar.

questions.q: Which scale should Nadine choose for the three views on her A3 sheet?
o: 1:5, as a larger scale is always clearer
1:10, the largest standard scale that fits
1:20, so there is plenty of room for notes and sizes
1:8, so the stand fills the sheet exactly
questions.why: At 1:10 the views need about 170 + 65 + 60 = 295 mm across and 90 + 65 + 60 = 215 mm down, so they fit; at 1:5 they would need about 530 mm across. 1:8 is not a standard scale, and 1:20 makes the views needlessly small.

questions.q: In the plan, the round drain hole in the sloping drip tray looks oval. Why?
o: The hole was drawn with the wrong compass setting
The plan is always drawn at a smaller scale than the front
The tray slopes, so the plan shows its face foreshortened
Holes are always drawn as ovals in a plan view
questions.why: A face that slopes to the viewing direction looks shorter than it is, so a circle on it appears as an ellipse. An auxiliary view looking square to the tray would show the hole as a true circle.

questions.q: How should Nadine show the side shelf in its folded-down position on the front view?
o: With a thin chain line that has two short dashes
With thick continuous lines like the other outlines
With thin dashed lines, as for hidden edges
With a freehand zigzag line round the shelf
questions.why: A thin chain line with two short dashes (long dash, double dot) shows other positions of moving parts and outlines of next-door parts. Dashed lines would wrongly say the shelf is hidden behind something.

questions.q: The welder measures the printed drip tray with a rule and works out a width from the 1:10 scale. No size is written for it. What is the right fix?
o: Let him use his measurement, since the print is to scale
Tell him to add 2 mm to allow for paper shrinking
Ask him to measure the pan and make the tray fit it
Add the missing size to the drawing and re-issue it
questions.why: Prints shrink and stretch, so a drawing must never be measured to find a size. Every size the workshop needs must be written on it; a missing size is a drawing error to correct and re-issue.

questions.q: Each chained size on Jodi-Ann's base plate may be 1 mm out. How far from its true position could the third hole end up?
o: Up to 3 mm
Up to 1 mm
Up to 2 mm
Up to 4 mm
questions.why: The left edge to hole 1, hole 1 to hole 2, and hole 2 to hole 3 are three chained sizes, and each may be 1 mm out, so the errors can add up to 3 mm. Dimensioning every hole from a datum keeps each one within 1 mm.

questions.q: Why should the overall width appear in only one view?
o: The width is only needed by the person cutting the plate
Giving it twice makes the drawing harder to print
If it changes, one of the two sizes may be missed
Only the plan view may carry overall sizes
questions.why: A size shown twice can be changed in one place and not the other, and then the drawing contradicts itself. Each size is given once, in the view that shows it best.

questions.q: The inspector measures four drilled holes in one plate. Which hole must be rejected?
o: The hole measuring 22.0 mm
The hole measuring 22.6 mm
The hole measuring 22.5 mm
The hole measuring 22.3 mm
questions.why: Ø22 +0.5/0 allows any size from 22.0 to 22.5 mm. A 22.6 mm hole is above the upper limit; the hole's own tolerance overrides the general ±1 mm.

questions.q: Jodi-Ann has corrected the errors you marked in red. What should happen before the drawing goes to the workshop?
o: She issues it at once, as the errors are now fixed
You check the corrections, then sign it as checked
Mr Clarke redraws it himself to make quite sure it is right
The welders check it when they start cutting the plates
questions.why: Corrections can bring in new errors, so the checker looks at them again before signing. The signed and dated checked box shows the drawing has been through checking.

questions.q: In section A–A, the stiffening plate is cut across and lies against the hopper side. How should the two cut parts be hatched?
o: In the same direction, so they look like one part
Only the hopper side is hatched, never the plate
In opposite directions, so the joint shows
With thick lines at 90°, to show they are welded
questions.why: Touching parts are hatched in opposite directions or at a different spacing so the reader can see where one ends. Hatching is always thin, and the same part keeps the same hatching in every view.

questions.q: At 1:10, the 3 mm sheet would be only 0.3 mm thick on the paper. How is it usually shown in the section?
o: Filled in solid black
With very close hatching
As a single thick line
Left out of the section
questions.why: Thin cut parts such as sheet and gaskets are filled in solid black because hatching cannot fit in them. A small white gap is left where two blacked-in parts touch.

questions.q: What angle separates the centres of neighbouring holes in the hopper's flange?
questions.why: Eight holes equally spaced round a full circle are 360 ÷ 8 = 45° apart. The pitch circle diameter (400 mm) fixes how far they are from the centre.

questions.q: The drafter must draw an auxiliary view of the sloping front to show the hatch at its true shape. From which view should it be projected?
o: From the plan, where the hatch looks shortest
From the view showing the front as an edge
From an isometric view of the whole hopper
From any view, since all views show the same sizes
questions.why: The auxiliary view is projected at 90° to the edge view of the sloping face. Depths are then transferred from the matching reference line in another view, so the hatch shows its true shape and size.

questions.q: How should the shop welds between the columns and their base plates be shown?
o: Fillet symbol, size 6, with a flag at the arrow's bend
A note saying WELD FULLY ROUND beside every column
Fillet symbol, size 6, with a circle at the arrow's bend
V-groove symbol, size 6, drawn below the reference line only
questions.why: The circle at the junction of the arrow and the reference line means weld all round, and the triangle with 6 gives a 6 mm fillet. A flag would mean a site weld, which these are not.

questions.q: On one bracing joint the fillet triangle is drawn above the reference line only. Where does the welder put the weld?
o: On the side of the joint the arrow touches
On both sides of the joint
On whichever side is easier to reach on site
On the side of the joint away from the arrow
questions.why: In the AWS system a symbol below the reference line means the arrow side, and above it the other side. The ISO system is read differently, so check which system a drawing uses.

questions.q: Dwight's print of Revision B is marked 1:20, but a 1000 mm column length measures 47 mm on it. What is the most likely cause?
o: It was printed using fit to page, not at 100%
The columns were drawn at 1:20 in model space
The dimension style was set up in the wrong units
The scale rule was read from the wrong side
questions.why: At 1:20, 1000 mm should measure 50 mm. A print set to fit the page is shrunk, so it no longer matches the title block. Print from the layout at 100%, then check a known size again.

questions.q: Several welders have photos of the Revision A sheets on their phones. What should be done when Revision B is issued?
o: Nothing, as the phone photos are only for their own use
Tell them B replaces A and to delete the old photos
Send them photos of B and let them keep A to compare
Ask them to write the new height on their Revision A prints
questions.why: An old revision on a phone is still an old revision, and someone may build from it. Issue B through the register, collect or mark the old copies, and make sure no copy of A stays in use.

questions.q: Where are the tangent points between the lug's straight sides and its R40 end?
o: At the two ends of the horizontal centre line through the hole
Where each straight side would first touch the edge of the Ø30 hole
Where a line from the centre, square to each side, meets the arc
Halfway along each side, between the base and the rounded end
questions.why: The tangent point between an arc and a straight line lies on the line drawn from the arc's centre at 90° to the straight line. Stopping the sides exactly there gives a smooth outline with no step.

questions.q: The pivot is cut from 24 mm across-flats hexagon bar. About how wide is it across the corners?
o: About 24.0 mm
About 27.7 mm
About 33.9 mm
About 20.8 mm
questions.why: Across corners is about 1.155 times across flats for a hexagon: 24 × 1.155 ≈ 27.7 mm. The across-flats size is the smaller one, measured between parallel faces.

questions.q: A gate's pivot pin is drawn Ø25 −0.05/−0.15 and its bush is bored Ø25 +0.10/0. What is the smallest clearance between them?
questions.why: The smallest clearance is the smallest hole (25.00 mm) minus the largest pin (24.95 mm), which is 0.05 mm. The largest clearance is 25.10 − 24.85 = 0.25 mm, so this is always a clearance fit.

questions.q: On an isometric drawing of a welded box, which lines are drawn at their true length?
o: Only the upright lines of the box
Every line, whatever its angle
Only the lines that run across the sheet
Lines parallel to the three axes
questions.why: In an isometric drawing, lengths along the upright axis and the two 30° axes are drawn true. Lines that are not parallel to an axis, such as a diagonal brace, are found by plotting their ends.
